title: DBMS Normalization
subject: Database Management Systems
blurb: Follow the normal forms as a chain of dependency repairs, from atomic values up to BCNF.

concepts.name: Functional Dependencies
concepts.summary: X -> Y means that any two rows agreeing on X must agree on Y. It is a statement about the data, not about the schema.
concepts.analogy: A dependency is a rule of the world: a PIN determines exactly one account, so PIN -> Account.
key_ideas: X -> Y holds when equal X implies equal Y
an FD is a property of the data, not the table layout
unnecessary FDs are the root cause of redundancy
worked: look at two rows with the same StudentID
if both rows always carry the same Name, then StudentID -> Name holds
ask the reverse: can two rows share a Name but have different StudentIDs? Yes - so Name -/-> StudentID
the arrow direction is the whole meaning; it is not symmetric

concepts.name: Keys: Superkey vs Candidate Key
concepts.summary: A superkey uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: drop any attribute and it stops being unique.
concepts.analogy: A full address identifies a house; the postcode alone does not. The full address is minimal only if no part can be dropped.
key_ideas: a superkey determines all attributes
a candidate key is a minimal superkey
a composite key has more than one attribute
worked: start with every attribute: {A, B, C} - that is a superkey
test minimality: is {A, B} still unique? yes -> drop C
test again: is {A} still unique? yes -> drop B
{A} is now minimal, so it is the candidate key

concepts.name: First Normal Form (1NF)
concepts.summary: Every attribute holds a single atomic value, and there are no repeating groups. 1NF says nothing about redundancy.
concepts.analogy: One item per box on a form. Not 'pens, notebooks' squeezed into a single field.
key_ideas: each cell holds one atomic value
no repeating groups or nested tables
1NF does not address redundancy
worked: bad: Orders(101, 'pen, notebook')
the Items cell holds two values in one field
split it: Orders(101, 'pen'), Orders(101, 'notebook')
each cell now holds exactly one atomic value - that is 1NF

concepts.name: Partial Dependency
concepts.summary: A non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key. It can only exist when the key has more than one attribute.
concepts.analogy: A recipe filed under both cuisine and dish, but the spice mix depends only on the cuisine - half the key is enough.
key_ideas: requires a composite key
the attribute depends on a proper subset of the key
single-column keys cannot have partial dependencies
worked: key is (StudentID, CourseID)
StudentName depends on StudentID alone - half the key
Grade depends on both StudentID and CourseID - the whole key
so StudentName is partially dependent; Grade is fully dependent

concepts.name: Second Normal Form (2NF)
concepts.summary: In 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole key, not part of it.
concepts.analogy: No half-dependencies. Every attribute has to justify both halves of the key.
key_ideas: 1NF plus no partial dependencies
only relevant when the key is composite
fix is to split the partially dependent attributes into their own table
worked: start from the 1NF table Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, Grade)
spot the partial dependency: StudentID -> StudentName
split it out: Student(StudentID, StudentName) and Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, Grade)
verify losslessness: joining on StudentID reproduces the original rows exactly

concepts.name: Transitive Dependency
concepts.summary: A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, which in turn depends on the key: key -> A -> B.
concepts.analogy: You know the department name because you know the department id, not because you know the employee.
key_ideas: key -> non-key -> non-key
the intermediate attribute is not a candidate key
this is what 3NF removes
worked: EmpID -> DeptID (the employee belongs to a department)
DeptID -> DeptName (a department has one name)
therefore EmpID -> DeptName, but only through DeptID
DeptName depends on the key indirectly, via a non-key attribute - that is transitive

concepts.name: Third Normal Form (3NF)
concepts.summary: In 2NF with no transitive dependencies: every non-key attribute depends directly on the key and nothing else.
concepts.analogy: Every fact in the table is about the key, and only about the key.
key_ideas: 2NF plus no transitive dependencies
fix is to move the transitively dependent pair into a new table
3NF still permits some redundancy
worked: start from Employee(EmpID, DeptID, DeptName) in 2NF
spot the transitive chain EmpID -> DeptID -> DeptName
split: Employee(EmpID, DeptID) and Department(DeptID, DeptName)
now every non-key attribute depends directly on its own table's key - that is 3NF

concepts.name: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
concepts.summary: Every determinant is a candidate key. Stricter than 3NF, and the price is that dependency preservation can be lost.
concepts.analogy: Nobody gets to be a boss unless they are also on the list of legitimate keys.
key_ideas: every determinant must be a candidate key
BCNF implies 3NF but not the reverse
decomposition is lossless but may not preserve all dependencies
worked: list the FDs: Student,Subject -> Teacher and Teacher -> Subject
list the candidate keys: (Student,Subject) and (Student,Teacher)
check every determinant: Teacher -> Subject has Teacher, which is not a candidate key
so the table is 3NF but not BCNF; decompose on Teacher
result: (Student,Teacher) and (Teacher,Subject) - lossless, and now every determinant is a key

misconceptions.name: You can jump straight to 3NF
misconceptions.statement: 3NF is the strictest of the classic forms, so checking it automatically covers 1NF and 2NF.
misconceptions.why: The normal forms are cumulative conditions, not a ladder you can skip. A table can satisfy a 3NF-style rule while still holding multi-valued cells, because 1NF was never checked.
misconceptions.repair: Walk the chain in order. Each form presupposes the one before it.

misconceptions.name: Partial and transitive dependencies are the same thing
misconceptions.statement: Both are dependencies you have to remove, so the distinction does not matter in practice.
misconceptions.why: Partial means depending on part of a composite key (a 2NF problem). Transitive means depending on a non-key attribute (a 3NF problem). They have different fixes and different symptoms.
misconceptions.repair: Ask what the attribute depends on. Part of the key -> partial. Another non-key attribute -> transitive.

misconceptions.name: Any unique column is a candidate key
misconceptions.statement: If a column has no duplicates it is a key, and a superkey and candidate key are the same idea.
misconceptions.why: Uniqueness makes it a superkey. Minimality makes it a candidate key. A composite superkey is not a candidate key if one of its attributes is already unique on its own.
misconceptions.repair: Test minimality explicitly: remove each attribute in turn and check whether uniqueness survives.

misconceptions.name: 3NF removes all redundancy
misconceptions.statement: Once a table is in 3NF there are no anomalies left.
misconceptions.why: 3NF permits anomalies when a non-key attribute determines another attribute but is not itself a candidate key. That is precisely the gap BCNF closes.
misconceptions.repair: Look for any determinant that is not a candidate key. If one exists, you are at 3NF but not BCNF.

misconceptions.name: Any normalized decomposition is safe
misconceptions.statement: If you split the table to remove a dependency, the result is automatically correct.
misconceptions.why: A decomposition must be lossless: joining the pieces back must reproduce exactly the original rows, no more and no fewer. It should also preserve dependencies, or you cannot enforce them without joining.
misconceptions.repair: Always verify losslessness by checking that the shared attribute of the two pieces is a key of at least one of them.

misconceptions.name: Comma-separated values are atomic enough
misconceptions.statement: A single cell containing 'pen, notebook' is one value, so the column is atomic.
misconceptions.why: A cell holding a list is a repeating group. It is not atomic, it cannot be indexed or constrained per element, and querying it means string surgery.
misconceptions.repair: If you would ever need to split the cell to answer a query, it is not atomic.

items.explain: The arrow is one-directional. It constrains rows that agree on the left, and says nothing about rows that agree on the right.

items.stem: In `Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName)`, which dependency causes redundancy?

options.text: StudentID -> StudentName, so the name repeats for every course the student takes
CourseID -> CourseID
(StudentID, CourseID) -> Grade
None - dependencies never cause redundancy

items.explain: Redundancy comes from a dependency whose determinant is not a key. The name is stored once per enrolment when it only needs storing once per student.

items.stem: What distinguishes a candidate key from a superkey?

options.text: A candidate key is minimal - removing any attribute destroys uniqueness
A candidate key must be a single column
A superkey is always smaller than a candidate key
Nothing; the terms are synonyms

items.explain: Every candidate key is a superkey, but not the reverse. Minimality is the whole distinction.

items.stem: In `R(A, B, C)` with FDs `A -> B` and `A -> C`, what are the candidate keys?

options.text: Just {A}
{A, B} and {A, C}
{A, B, C}
{B, C}

items.explain: A alone determines everything, so adding anything to it makes the set non-minimal. Only {A} is a candidate key.

options.text: Orders(OrderID, Items) where Items holds 'pen, notebook'
Orders(OrderID, ItemName) with one row per item
Orders(OrderID, CustomerID)
Orders(OrderID, Total)

items.explain: A list inside a cell is a repeating group. One row per item is the 1NF shape.

options.text: No - it is about atomic values and no repeating groups; redundancy is addressed later
Yes, 1NF removes all duplicate data
Yes, 1NF requires every column to be a key
1NF only applies to numeric columns

items.explain: This is the most common misconception about 1NF. Atomicity is a structural property; redundancy is a dependency property.

items.stem: `Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, Grade)` with key (StudentID, CourseID). Which is a partial dependency?

options.text: StudentID -> StudentName, since it depends on only part of the key
(StudentID, CourseID) -> Grade, since it needs the whole key
StudentName -> Grade
There is none in this table

items.explain: Depending on the whole key is exactly what you want. Depending on half of it is the defect.

items.stem: Why can a table with a single-column primary key never have a partial dependency?

options.text: A partial dependency needs a composite key to be partial against
Single-column keys are automatically in 2NF
Partial dependencies only occur with foreign keys
It can - any FD on a small key counts as partial

items.explain: There is no proper non-empty subset of a single attribute, so there is nothing for the dependency to be partial to.

options.text: 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key
1NF plus no transitive dependency
Only atomic values
BCNF

items.explain: 2NF is the partial-dependency rule. Transitive dependencies are 3NF's business.

items.stem: After decomposing a table to remove a partial dependency, what else must you verify?

options.text: That the decomposition is lossless and preserves dependencies
That the new tables have more rows than before
Nothing - 2NF guarantees correctness
That every new table has a surrogate key

items.explain: Normalization is not finished when the anomaly disappears. You must be able to rebuild the original relation by joining.

items.stem: `Employee(EmpID, DeptID, DeptName)` with `EmpID -> DeptID -> DeptName`. How does DeptName relate to EmpID?

options.text: Transitively dependent on EmpID, through DeptID
Partially dependent on EmpID
Fully dependent on EmpID
Independent of EmpID

items.explain: The dependency path has a non-key hop in the middle. That hop is what makes it transitive rather than direct.

items.stem: How do you remove that transitive dependency?

options.text: Move DeptID and DeptName into a separate Department table
Delete the DeptName column
Make (EmpID, DeptID) the composite primary key
Copy DeptName into every row for faster reads

items.explain: The fix relocates the dependency, it does not delete information. DeptName belongs with DeptID, not with the employee.

options.text: 2NF plus no transitive dependency on a non-key attribute
2NF plus atomic values
No functional dependencies at all
That every determinant is a candidate key

items.explain: The last option is the definition of BCNF, which is the trap in this question. 3NF is the weaker condition.

items.stem: Can a table in 3NF still contain redundancy?

options.text: Yes - when a non-key attribute determines another attribute
No - 3NF removes all redundancy
Only if it has no primary key
Only for numeric columns

items.explain: This is the exact gap BCNF exists to close. 3NF permits a determinant that is not a candidate key.

options.text: Every determinant must be a candidate key
It forbids composite keys
It requires 4NF to be checked first
It permits transitive dependencies

items.explain: 3NF only restricts dependencies whose right-hand side is a non-key attribute. BCNF restricts every determinant, key or not.

items.stem: `Teach(Student, Subject, Teacher)` where each Subject has exactly one Teacher and each Student takes one Subject at a time. Which form does it violate?

options.text: BCNF - Teacher -> Subject, but Teacher is not a candidate key
1NF - the values are not atomic
2NF - there is a partial dependency
Nothing, it is already in BCNF

items.explain: The candidate keys are (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher). Teacher determines Subject but is not a key, which is precisely the BCNF violation.

options.text: Losslessness, but not necessarily dependency preservation
Both losslessness and dependency preservation
Neither
Better query performance

items.explain: This is the honest cost of BCNF, and a favourite exam question. Sometimes you must accept 3NF to keep dependencies enforceable.

items.stem: What is the usual trade-off when you normalize a table into 3NF?

options.text: Fewer anomalies, but more joins to reassemble the data
More redundancy but fewer joins
Both writes and reads get slower
No trade-off - normalization is free

items.explain: Normalization moves the cost from maintenance to query time. Knowing that is what lets you denormalize deliberately rather than by accident.
